items.prompt: Two implementations of the same function both pass every test. What does this tell you about their design quality (coupling, cohesion, future change cost)?
choices: Passing tests proves both have equally good design
Nothing directly — correctness (does it produce the right output) and design quality (how much future changes will cost) are different properties; code can be fully correct and still badly designed
Passing tests proves the better-designed one is faster
Design quality can only be assessed by counting lines of code
items.explanation: Correctness and design quality are explicitly separated in this unit — tests verify output for given inputs, not how expensive the next change will be. Both implementations in L3 are equally correct; they differ sharply in what adding a new notification channel costs.

items.prompt: What does "high coupling" between two pieces of code mean?
choices: They are stored in the same file
They are entangled such that changing one is likely to force changes in the other, often because one reaches into the other's internal implementation details rather than a stable interface
They share a common naming convention
They were written by the same developer
items.explanation: Coupling measures entanglement, not proximity or authorship. The L2 example shows OrderService reaching into EmailService's smtpClient internals directly — a change to EmailService's implementation can break OrderService even though nothing about OrderService's actual job (completing orders) changed.

items.prompt: Per L2, what's the actual test for whether a module has good cohesion?
choices: Whether all its methods touch the same variable or object type
Whether all its methods change for the same reason — not just whether they're superficially related to a common subject
Whether the module is under 50 lines long
Whether the module has a single public method
items.explanation: L2's low-cohesion OrderProcessor example has all three methods touching `order`, which looks related — but pricing logic, email copy, and analytics schema are independent reasons to change, so bundling them still counts as low cohesion. The real test is shared reason to change, not surface-level topical relatedness.

items.prompt: Per L2's cost curve, why do the poorly-designed and well-designed lines start at roughly the same cost for early changes, then diverge later?
choices: Early changes are always trivial regardless of design, so the divergence is an illusion

Bad design's cost compounds — each change has to work around entanglement left by every previous change — while well-designed code's structure doesn't actively fight the next change, keeping cost closer to flat over time
The well-designed version is simply written by more experienced developers
The curves only diverge if the codebase changes programming languages
items.explanation: This is exactly why bad design's cost is easy to miss upfront: it's invisible on the first few changes and only becomes visible as accumulated entanglement makes each subsequent change more expensive than the last — a compounding effect, not a one-time cost.

items.prompt: A system will only ever need one notification channel, with no plausible future requirement for a second. Per L3's failure modes, is building the pluggable `notifiers` array abstraction upfront still a good idea?
choices: Yes — more abstraction is always safer, regardless of actual need
No — with no real second channel expected, the abstraction is pure cost with no payoff; the decoupled design is only worth its complexity because a second channel was a real, concrete requirement
Yes, because it makes the code shorter
No, because pluggable abstractions are always a code smell in every context
items.explanation: L3 explicitly calls this over-engineering: design investment should match expected future change, not be applied uniformly regardless of whether that change is actually likely. Building for a hypothetical second channel that never arrives just adds indirection with no corresponding benefit.

items.prompt: Implement `completeOrder(order, notifiers)` in the decoupled style from L3: it should call `.notify(order)` on every notifier in the `notifiers` array (in order) and return an array of their return values — `OrderService` itself should never need to know how many notifiers there are or what they do.

tests.description: calls notify on a single notifier and returns its result
calls notify on every notifier, in order, collecting all results
with zero notifiers, returns an empty array without erroring

items.explanation: OrderService-equivalent code only ever calls the shared `.notify(order)` interface — it never inspects what kind of notifier it's talking to or how many there are. Adding a new notifier type (SMS, push, Slack) never requires touching this function again, which is the entire point of the decoupled design from L3: the change is additive, not invasive.
